description: Sabotages for tools/check-test-tiers.ps1, the check that a test's ignore reason and its module agree about which tier it is in, judged by test-check-test-tiers.ps1. Run with tools/run-sabotage.ps1 -Manifest tools/sabotage-tiers.json -CargoCommand tools/sabotage-tiers-runner.cmd; see tools/README-sabotage.md.

sabotages.name: a marked test outside its tier's module is accepted
sabotages.why: The tier's run selects by the module name, so a test marked long-haul that sits anywhere else is one nothing runs: it is skipped on every push and never picked up by the run that exists for it, and the build stays green.

sabotages.name: a marker with nothing after it is accepted
sabotages.why: The text after the marker is where what a test costs is written. A bare marker passes the selection and leaves a reader of the ignore list nothing to judge it by.

sabotages.name: an unmarked test in a tier module is accepted
sabotages.why: A test in the module that is not ignored runs on every push although it was meant for the tier; one ignored for another reason is picked up by the tier's run for a reason that is not its own. Both are the same unmarked test.

sabotages.name: a path that only contains the filter is accepted
sabotages.why: libtest's filter is a substring match, so `long_haul::` also selects `not_long_haul::t`. Without this check a test is swept into a tier by the spelling of an unrelated module.

sabotages.name: a misspelt marker is accepted
sabotages.why: `Long-haul:` or `long_haul:` is meant as the marker and is not one, so the test is ignored for a reason the tier does not recognise and nothing says so.

sabotages.name: the module name is matched without regard to case
sabotages.why: libtest's filter is case-sensitive, so a module spelt `Long_Haul` is never selected by `long_haul::`. PowerShell's `-contains` ignores case and would call it in the module, which is the wrong answer exactly where the check exists to be right.

sabotages.name: the test's own name counts as one of its modules
sabotages.why: The filter `long_haul::` selects a path with a segment of that name FOLLOWED by another, so a test that is itself called `long_haul` is not selected. Counting the last segment as a module accepts it.

sabotages.name: the marker is matched without regard to case
sabotages.why: The marker is spelt one way so that it can be searched for. Accepting `Long-haul:` makes the spelling a matter of who wrote the test, and it is the lookalike rule that would have said so.

sabotages.name: a target with its own harness is ignored
sabotages.why: The check runs every test executable with libtest's arguments; one with `harness = false` would run its own main instead. The refusal exists so that is a decision made here and not something found in a CI run.

sabotages.name: a build that failed is not noticed
sabotages.why: A census taken over tests that did not build saw fewer tests than exist and would pass for the wrong reason. The exit code is what says the build worked.

sabotages.name: a test that breaks a rule exits zero
sabotages.why: The exit code is the only thing CI reads.

sabotages.name: a missing listing exits zero
sabotages.why: A census that could not be taken must not look like one that found nothing wrong.

sabotages.name: a line libtest wrote with an unescaped backslash reads every test as not ignored
sabotages.why: libtest does not escape a backslash in an ignore reason, so a reason that names a path (the administrative-share tests have one) is not valid JSON and is read by shape. A reading that gets `ignore` wrong turns a marked test into an unmarked one in its module.

sabotages.name: a line libtest wrote with an unescaped backslash loses its reason
sabotages.why: The same reading, losing the text: the marker is the start of the reason, so a reason read as empty is an unmarked test.

sabotages.name: a workflow command that runs every ignored test is not read
sabotages.why: A cargo test line with --include-ignored or --ignored selects every ignored test it is not told to skip, which includes the tiers, so a push would run them. The check reads those lines; without it nothing notices one.

sabotages.name: --ignored alone is not read as selecting ignored tests
sabotages.why: `--ignored` runs the ignored tests just as `--include-ignored` does, so a command that spells it that way selects the tiers too.

sabotages.name: a skip is not honoured
sabotages.why: A command that skips the tiers by name selects none of them, and one that skips only one selects the other; a check that ignored the skips would refuse the commands that are right.

sabotages.name: a name filter is not honoured
sabotages.why: A command with a name filter selects only the tests whose names contain it, so one naming other tests selects no tier test; a check that ignored the filters would refuse it.

sabotages.name: the packages a command names are not honoured
sabotages.why: A command with -p selects that package's tests and no other's; a check that took every package would refuse a command for a package that has no tier test.

sabotages.name: the targets a command names are not honoured
sabotages.why: A command with --test or --lib selects only those executables; a check that took every target would refuse a command for a target that holds no tier test.

sabotages.name: an exact name is matched as a part of one
sabotages.why: Under --exact a name selects only the test of that whole name, so a name that is only part of a tier test's selects nothing of it.

sabotages.name: CONTROL: the problems are listed in another order
sabotages.why: The manifest checking itself. This changes the order a reader sees problems in and nothing a test claims, so it MUST survive -- if it comes back caught, the suite is matching on incidental ordering rather than behaviour, and its other results are worth less than they look.
